appraisal_events.evidence: "C'est le seul arrondissement où le pauvre général n'a jamais échoué" — the duchesse puns his repeated electoral failures against his wife's repeated pregnancies.
appraisal_events.explanation: The duchesse extends her running mockery of the general's failures into a bawdy quip, again diminishing him while displaying her own wit.

appraisal_events.evidence: The narrator is thereafter continually invited to the Guermantes' dinners, presented to their friends "avec une nuance de bienveillance si marquée" that no host would dare give a ball without including him; his taste is admired when he has cherry and pear juice added to the traditional orangeade, and général de Monserfeuil later bows to him "comme si j'eusse été président du Conseil supérieur de la guerre."
appraisal_events.explanation: Across the passage the narrator recounts, in his own endorsed retrospective voice, his sustained absorption into the innermost circle of the Guermantes' social world and the marked favor shown him there.

appraisal_events.evidence: "Ce fut par la véritable méchanceté de Mme de Guermantes que je fus révolté" when, as the princesse de Parme timidly offers to speak to Monserfeuil herself on Robert's behalf despite his dangerous posting, the duchesse does everything she can to dissuade her, claiming Monserfeuil "n'a aucune espèce de crédit ni de pouvoir avec le nouveau gouvernement."
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator names and condemns outright the duchesse's true malice in actively blocking help for her endangered nephew, a sharp escalation from mere unhelpfulness to deliberate cruelty.

status_effects.explanation: He is again the butt of a mocking pun about his repeated failures.
Her quick bawdy pun again displays her command of the conversational register.
He is described as marked out for sustained, visible favor within the Guermantes' circle, his taste and influence explicitly admired by others.
He crosses fully into the innermost, habitual circle of Guermantes guests, to the point that hosts feel obliged to include him on every list.
The narrator explicitly names her true malice in sabotaging help for her endangered nephew, a strong and clearly endorsed condemnation.
Her timid, well-meaning offer to help is skillfully talked down by the duchesse, leaving her overridden despite her goodwill and superior rank.
